message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This evaluation gives us, for the first time, a clean side-by-side comparison of schools with and without reminders across a full season, using the immunisation team's own vaccination records rather than survey data. The headline is striking: a 13-point uptake advantage in reminder schools, with consent return clearly identified as the bottleneck, since over 92% of consented children were vaccinated in both groups. That tells us exactly where to intervene, and text reminders act directly on consent. It is also good news that Eastvale reached 66% overall uptake, above the national 65% ambition for the first time, so we are building on success. The cost analysis is deliberately cautious, assuming every reminder goes to every non-consenting family, and still comes in under £5,000. I have looked hard for reasons not to scale this and have not found any: it is cheap, quick to deploy and the effect size is large. Extending it to all 92 schools is the obvious next step.
</author>

<document>
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.
</document>
response:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders Evaluation, 2025-26

The cost case is sound, but two of the report's central claims don't hold up. The 66% headline figure contradicts the report's own table, and the "13 points caused by reminders" conclusion isn't supported by a self-selected comparison. The author's summary repeats both claims.

## 1. The 66% overall uptake figure is wrong

Table 1's own numbers give 13,772 / 22,080 = **62.4%**, not 66.0%. The two group rows check out (6,384/9,120 = 70.0%, 7,388/12,960 = 57.0%). Even a simple average of 70 and 57 gives 63.5%, so no reading of the table gets to 66%.

- Eastvale did **not** exceed the 65% national ambition. It fell about 2.6 points short.
- The "first time above the ambition" line appears in the report and the author's summary, so it should be corrected before this goes to the Board.
- Someone should also check where 66% came from, in case other figures were drawn from the same source.

Minor: non-reminder consent return is 7,970/12,960 = 61.5%, which the report rounds to 61%.

## 2. The 13-point gap is not evidence that reminders caused the effect

The report says the difference "shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points". Schools opted in, and the report itself shows that opting-in schools differ systematically:

- **School nurse:** 29 of 38 reminder schools (76%) had a full-time nurse, against 11 of 54 (20%) of the others. A nurse could plausibly raise consent return without any texts.
- **Affluence and geography:** reminder schools are mostly in the affluent west. Non-reminder schools include the eastern wards with more multilingual and mobile households.
- **Contact data:** valid mobile numbers are held for 93% of families in reminder schools but only 61% in the others. This is a difference in baseline infrastructure.
- **Motivated schools:** schools that choose to opt in are probably more engaged generally.

Nothing here lets us separate the reminder effect from these factors. The real effect could be 13 points, much less, or occasionally more. "Clean side-by-side comparison" overstates the design, since using administrative records rather than survey data fixes measurement but not selection. There was also no pre-intervention baseline, so we can't tell whether reminder schools already had higher uptake in 2024-25.

The claim that reminders beat "any other intervention we have tried" has no comparison anywhere in the report. The only other intervention mentioned is mop-up sessions (+3 to 6 points), and those aren't compared on a like-for-like basis.

## 3. The forecast of 70% in non-reminder schools is unsafe

The recommendation assumes the same 13-point gain will carry over to a very different population. Specific problems:

- Only **61%** of families in those schools have a valid mobile number, so up to 39% can't be reached at all. The cost estimate assumes every non-consenting family gets texts, but the benefit estimate should be scaled down for the same reason.
- The text links to an online portal. For families with language barriers or high mobility, and in schools where paper forms come back incomplete, a link may not solve the problem. The report doesn't say whether messages are multilingual.
- Non-reminder uptake ranges from 38% to 79%, so one school already exceeds the reminder-school average. This shows large variation from other causes.
- "Bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" is likely to be the opposite of what happens: the lowest-uptake schools may benefit least. This could widen rather than close the equity gap.

## 4. The consent-bottleneck point is reasonable but weaker than presented

Conversion from consent to vaccination is 93% in reminder schools and 92.7% in the others, so consent is where most children are lost. That is a sensible reading. But it only says where the gap arises, not that texting is what closes it. Also, 7% of consented children go unvaccinated, which is around 1,000 children and isn't trivial. Mop-up sessions would address this, and they were run in only 14 schools.

## 5. Costs

The arithmetic is correct: about £1,198 for the 54 schools, £547 for the existing 38, and £2,500 set-up gives roughly **£4,250**, under £5,000. Remarks:

- It is "cautious" only on the cost side. Benefits are not treated cautiously.
- It omits staff time, the cost of cleaning and collecting mobile numbers (essential given the 61% coverage), translation, and the vaccine and nurse cost of the additional children vaccinated.
- Cost per additional vaccinated child can't be calculated without a credible effect estimate, so that figure should be given as a range.

## 6. Other points

- The report is dated February 2026 and recommends funding from September 2026, which has now passed. Check the current status before reusing the timetable.
- The author says they "looked hard for reasons not to scale this and have not found any". The points above are such reasons, and the report itself contains most of the evidence for them.

## Suggested changes

1. Correct the overall uptake to 62.4% and remove the claim of exceeding the national ambition.
2. Reword to say reminder schools had 13 points higher uptake, and that the difference is **associated with** reminders but confounded by nurse presence, area and contact data. Drop "more than any other intervention".
3. If possible, compare within strata (nurse/no nurse, west/east) and against 2024-25 uptake by school.
4. Present the rollout as a staged expansion, ideally randomising or phasing the order of the 54 schools so the effect can be measured. Reminders are cheap, so scaling is defensible. The issue is the strength of the claim, not the decision to try.
5. Pair reminders with a plan to collect mobile numbers, provide translated messages, and prioritise mop-up sessions in the eastern schools.
6. Give a range for expected uptake rather than a single 70% figure, and include the omitted costs.
